Similar to the original SAME investigation, the primary objective of the SAME-R investigation was to quantify the sizes that the liquid smoke particulate achieves in low gravity and to relate the droplet size distribution to the smoke generation and smoke transport conditions in the experiment. One of the problems encountered during the SAME investigation was that after the thermal precipitators were returned to the ground, it was found that all the TEM grids were severely contaminated with some unidentified foreign particles, making these grids unusable although some of them showed shapes of certain types of smoke particles. Based on that experience the SAME-R investigation employed several modification covering new materials, extended operating conditions, and diagnostic equipments.

SAME-R utilized the SAME hardware used on-orbit. Based on the experience gained from SAME, SAME-R included the following modifications: 1) a new test material,
Pyrell®, an intumescent fire-retardant foam by Foamex, was introduced to replace DBP samples, 2) test conditions were broadened including higher heating temperatures and no-flow during sample heating time, and 3) a new instrument, M-pass, developed in-house GRC, was used to replace one of the two Commercial Diagnostic Enclosures that includes a DustTrak and an ionization detector used in SAME. SAME-R flight tests were conducted from July 16, to September 9, 2010, successfully completing 66 test points. After SAME-R flight tests, three major post–flight ground tests were performed to improve data reduction process and to validate the lognormal distribution assumption, the key to the moment method employed by SAME and SAME-R.

The three hypotheses that motivated the original SAME investigation is also applicable for the reflight SAME-R investigation:
In a μg environment, with the absence of the strong buoyancy-induced flows, smoke particle growth from a pyrolyzing/smoldering source, as a result of nucleation, condensation, and coagulation, will lead to larger particles compared to those produced in 1g. The formation of the larger particles is favored by the expected higher vapor concentration and smoke residence times near the source due to the reduced velocities and mixing at μg conditions. In particular, it is hypothesized that liquid aerosol smokes produced in microgravity will exhibit substantially larger droplet sizes than under the same conditions in normal gravity (with a corresponding decrease in the particle number density for the same mass of smoke). The change in the size distribution and number density will, in turn, affect the response of the smoke detectors and possibly result in some detectors not producing an alarm when exposed to this smoke.

Along with the results from the original SAME investigation, the results from SAME-R can lead to technology for an advanced fire detector for future spacecraft that will be used for long duration missions. SAME will provide quantitative data on the sensitivity of these detectors to reduced gravity smokes that will allow evaluation of the adequacy of these existing technologies using relevant data. The current Fire Prevention, Detection, and Suppression (FPDS) program plan allows for the re-evaluation of future sensor technology, to allow new technology and capability to be utilized. The results from SAME are needed to provide the reduced gravity baseline data against which future detection technology developments can be evaluated. The smoke detectors developed from the results of SAME can also be useful in other extreme environments on Earth, such as submarines or underwater laboratories. Accurate detection of smoke in these environments can save lives.

Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment Re-flight (SAMER) 
 
 
Abstract 
 
Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment Re-flight (SAMER) is an extension or continuation of Smoke Aerosol 
Measurement Experiment (SAME), conducted in space from  September 9 to October 5, 2007. On the success of 
SAME, SAMER included the following modifications: 1) a new test sample material Pyrell ®, an intumescent fire-
retardant foam by Foamex was introduced to replace DBP samples, 2) test condition ranges was extended to include 
higher heating temperature and no-flow conditions, and 3) a new instrument, M-pass, developed in-house GRC, was 
used to replace one of the two Commercial Diagnostic Enclosures used in SAME. SAMER flight tests were 
conducted from July 16, to September 9, 2010, successfully completing 66 test  points. As a part of SAMER effort, 
three major post–flight ground tests were performed: the SAMER apparatus flow tests to obtain accurate dilution 
ratio data, the TEM tests to obtain the 1-g counterpart of TEM samples and a batch of SMPS tests to examine the 
validity of the lognormal distribution assumption of aerosol  particle size for the tested materials. Based on the 
results of both SAMER flight and ground-based tests, it is concluded that the moment method in conjunction the 
lognormal distribution assumption is a valid and effective approach to characterization of the aerosol encountered in 
space vehicles. Particle size distributio ns of aerosol produced from 5 tested materials commonly found in space 
crafts were identified.  
 
Introduction 
 
Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment Re-flight (SAMER) is one of the awarded Rapid Turn Around (RTA) 
projects, solicited by NASA Headquarters in June 2009. SAMER is an extension or continuation of Smoke Aerosol 
Measurement Experiment (SAME), which was conducted in the Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) onboard 
the International Space Station (ISS) from September 9 to October 5, 2007. 
 
Generally speaking, SAME experiments were completed successfully in that the apparatus developed for the 
experiments functioned well and desired data from instruments were obtained. However, there was a major problem 
of the SAME experiments. After the thermal precipitators returned to the ground, it was found that all the TEM grids 
were severely contaminated with some unidentified foreign particles, making these grids unusable although some of 
them showed shapes of certain types of smoke particles.  
 
Based on the experience gained from SAME, SAMER included the following modifications: 1) a new test material, 
Pyrell®, an intumescent fire-retardant foam  by Foamex, was introduced to repl ace DBP samples, 2) test conditions 
were broadened including higher heating temperatures and no-flow during sample heating time, and 3) a new 
instrument, M-pass, developed in-house GRC, was used to replace one of the two Commercial Diagnostic 
Enclosures that includes a DustTrak and an ionization detector used in SAME. SAMER flight tests were conducted 
from July 16, to September 9, 2010, successfully completing 66 test points. 
 
After SAMER flight tests, three major post–flight ground tests were performed to improve data reduction process 
and to validate the lognormal distribution assumption, the key to the moment method employed by SAME and 
SAMER. The first ground-based test is the SAMER apparatu s flow tests. The objective of the test is to obtain 
accurate dilution ratio data of the P-trak and Dusttrak so that the accuracy of aerosol concentration can be improved. 
The second batch of ground tests was the TEM tests which were conducted under exactly the same conditions as 
those for the SAMER flight tests so that the gravity effects on the TEM samples can be identified. The third batch of 
ground tests was to a SMPS apparatus to obtain the actual particle size distribution under the same condition as the 
SAMER flight tests. The objective of these tests is to ex amine the validity of lognormal particle size distribution 
assumption.  
 
Besides these ground tests, there were two improvements in the data reduction procedures. One is to derive sample 
heating temperatures from the logged engineering data so th at each test can be characterized by the sample heating 
temperature instead of R t/R0 as has always been used. It was reali zed that even two tests use the same R t/R0, the 
sample heating temperatures can be quite different. Charac terizing a test with sample heating temperature makes it

easier to understand the particle generation from the view point of material pyrolysis. The second improvement is to 
device a method of calculating the percentage of cumulative moment detected by an instrument that has a limited 
particle size detection range. This development allows us to improve uncertainty analysis of the results we obtained. 
 
Since the apparatus used in SAMER is mostly unchanged from that of SAME and the basic approach – the moment 
method – used by the two experiments are the same, in this report, these two parts – the apparatus and the moment 
methods – will not be repeated. What w ill be included in this final report are the newly added part, the improved 
data reduction methods and the new results of particle distributions.

Six re-assembled Thermal Precipitators, each having 12 TEM grids in it, were uploaded to ISS for SAMER. 
 
Since the SAMER project is a re-flight of SAME, the ha rdware, the project approach, the principle of moment 
method, post flight data analysis and uncertainty analysis will not be repeated  in this report. Information in these 
areas can be found in the final report of the original SAME project. This re port emphasizes information unique for

The SAME-R flight operation was carried out from July 16, 2010 to September 9, 2010 in 7 time periods: July 16, 
July 19-22, July 29-30, August 2, August 23-27, August 30 and September 7-9. Totally 67 runs were conducted 
including two runs using reused samples. The test conditions of each run can be found in Appendix A, where the 
secondary aging runs are listed as separate entities, making th e total run number to 109. In the SAMER flight tests, 
70 TEM samples were collected totally. 
 
During the tests, SAMER engineer team and science team  were in the Tele-Science Center in GRC, where they 
could communicate with the astronaut who is conducting the test and have a real time video of the apparatus when

space to ground signal transmission is available. The engineering hous ekeeping data files generated during the tests 
were downlinked shortly after tests were completed each da y. The entire flight test op eration was quite smooth and 
as planned. The hardware worked fine without any unexpected events. 
 
After entire SAMER tests were completed, the six carousel s, all tested samples and the six thermal precipitators 
were shipped to the GRC for measuring sample weight losses and TEM grid analysis.  
 
 
SAMER results 
The preliminary results of SAMER experiments are best summarized in a paper titled “Particle Morphology and 
Size results from the Smoke Aerosol M easurement Experiment-2” [ref. xx]. Be low are excerpts fr om the relevant 
part of the paper. The referenced materials that are beyond the text of excerpts can be found in the original paper. 
 
Over 100 sample materials were tested.  These were comprised of samples of 6 materials: Teflon™, Kapton™, 
Pyrell™, silicone rubber, cellulose (lamp wick), and dibutyl-phthalate deposited on a porous wick. The test 
conditions included multiple sample temperatures and air flow rates.  The baseline air flow rate was 8 cm/s with 
runs conducted at rates down to 2 cm/s with a limited set conducted with no airflow while the sample was heated.  
The sample temperatures were based on the pyrolysis properties of the material and were thus material specific.  The 
baseline temperature was selected to produce 1 to 2 mg of weight loss in 60 seconds and have reasonable signal on 
each of the moment instruments.  To examine the effect of sample temper ature, additional higher temperature 
conditions were also selected that would not saturate th e moment instruments. The TEM girds recovered from the 
thermal precipitators on SAME-1 were unfortunately cont aminated with extraneous particles whose origin is 
currently under investigation. For SAME-2 more rigorous assembly controls were followed and numerous good 
particle images were obtained.  For typical runs, the partic le concentrations were a few million particles / cc and the 
mass concentrations were 2 to 15 mg/m 3 however there were runs with fewer particles.  For these conditions, the 
typical numbers of particles sampled by the instruments were in the billions although for the test with the lowest 
particle concentrations the sample sizes were of the order of several million particles. 
 
A. Moment Instrument Results 
Geometric mean, count mean, and average mass diameter re sults from the moment instruments for baseline runs 
are presented in Table 1.  As desc ribed above, the count mean diameter  and the diameter of average mass 
measurements are independent of the nature of the size distribution however, the calculation of the geometric mean 
diameter and the geometric standard deviation ( σg) depend on the assumption of a log-normal distribution.  This 
assumption cannot be directly tested with the available da ta since this would require a device that can separate the 
particles into size bins.  However, there are two indications that the distribution can be approximated by a log-
normal distribution.  In the cases listed below, the count mean diameter is less than the diameter of average mass 
which is a necessary condition for a log-normal distribution (See Fig. 1).  The second indication is that the geometric 
standard deviations are all physically reasonable (i.e. greater than 1 (see Eq. 3) and less than approximately 3.5 
which is the practical limit on the magnitude of aerosol ge ometric standard deviation).  The aging results show a 
substantial increase in the observed diam eters.  As expected the increase in th e count mean diameter is greater than 
the corresponding increase in th e diameter of average mass.  This can be understood since coagulation consists of 
particle collisions joining two particles.  For a polydisper se aerosol, these collisions usually involve the collision of 
one of the smallest (high mobility) particles with the larg est (high cross-section) par ticles. This collision has little 
effect on the size of the large particle but it removes the smaller particles from the size distribution.  This has a 
larger effect on the count mean diameter since it is linear in diameter while the diameter of average mass varies with 
the cube root of the diameter. Theoretical predictions suggest that this process will produce a near lognormal 
distribution and that the standard deviation will tend toward a self-preserving distribution with a value of 1.32.14

Overall, the Teflon and Kapton particles were very small.  The lamp wick and silicone results exhibited 
substantially larger diameters of average mass, partic ularly for the aged cases.  As reported previously 10, the Dust

Teflon will make detection of this smoke challenging for light scattering devices, on the other hand the large sizes 
seen with the lamp wick and silicone would generate very large signals on a light scattering system.  As discussed

signal from small particles such as Teflon and Kapton without excessive nuisance alarms from large dust particles is 
difficult without some level of particle size discrimination.  This suggests that detection of these particles against the 
background environment will require a detection system capable of measuring more than one moment of the particle 
size distribution.

B. MPASS Results 
The MPASS was included in SAME-2 to demonstrate the effectiveness of a two-moment smoke detector. 
Because of how they are used, a smoke  detector is not calibrated for speci fic materials and instead has a single 
calibration for all conditions. The objective is to maintain a flat sensor response, regardless of the type of smoke or 
the particle size so the signal is proportional only to a se lected moment (e.g. mass or number concentration).  The 
approach used was to derive correlations to predict the smoke number concentration and mass concentration from 
the MPASS output.  This correlation was made using the other SAME measurements (number and mass 
concentration) as a reference.  A least-squares, third-order, correlation was computed on all test points with a signal 
to noise ratio greater than 2 independent of all other parameters (e.g. material, heating rate, and aging time).

The MPASS therefore has the ability to discern the difference between a strong signal from a high smoke 
concentration and a strong signal from a lower concentration of very large dust particles, a feature which can 
minimize false smoke detector alarms.   
 
 
 
 
C. TEM Results

precipitator.  These samples were imaged with a TEM to evaluate the particle morphology as a function of flow 
conditions, material and heating level.  Overall, silicone rubber presented no particles that were visible via TEM, 
presumably because the particles were condensed liquid that evaporated before they coul d be imaged in the TEM.

D. Impact of flow on particle morphology 
As the samples are heated by the wire, chemical bonds are broken and gaseous products are released via pyrolysis.  
These products may include partially oxidized species resulting from the reaction with oxygen. As the gases move 
from the wire, the temperature and species concentration will decrease as a result of conduction/diffusion and 
convection.  With the decrease in temperature, the super saturation ratio of the pyrolysis gas will pass a critical stage 
and nucleation of smoke particles will occur.  These smoke nuclei grow rapidly from the condensation of the 
pyrolysis gases.  The time scale for the nucleation and condensation is on the order of miliseconds or less.  Over a 
longer time scale, the growing smoke particles undergoing Brownian motion collide and stick together in a process 
known as coagulation.  This process may continue for time scales of up to thousand seconds.  If the particles are 
liquid, the colliding particles will coalesce and form larger droplets.  This is the case for the lampwick, silicone 
rubber, and Kapton smokes (Fig. 11).  If the particles are solid, they will retain their structure as they stick resulting 
in an agglomerate structure composed of many primary particles connected in a low density fractal-like structure.  
This is the case for the Teflon and Pyrell smokes (Fig. 11). 
 
Key parameters affecting the smoke properties of the smoke produced here are the low-gravity condition, the 
convective flow past the heated wire, the wire temperature, and the aging time.  As the wire temperature increases, 
more of the sample will be pyrolyzed and these gases will subsequently condense on the nuclei leading to a larger 
mass concentration of the aerosol and a larger diameter of average mass.   
 
An increase in the convective flow for a fixed wire temperature is expected to result in an increase in the pyrolysis 
rate and thus an increase in the mass concentration of the aerosol.  Some results follow this trend with silicone 
rubber, lampwick, and Pyrell increasing slightly with flow while Teflon and Kapton decrease.  A possible 
explanation is that holding the wire temperature fixed does not necessarily mean that the sample surface temperature 
distribution is precisely the same at different air flow speeds.  Although these are expected to be small variations, 
given the exponential dependence of the pyrolysis kinetics on temperature, changes in the heat transport 
environment could change the sample surface temperature between the wire coils.   
 
A case of special interest is the case of zero-flow.  The transport for the zero-flow case in μ-g is controlled by 
molecular diffusion and thermal expansion.  Over a period of 60 seconds, the gases would diffuse a distance on the 
order of 4 cm.  Assuming a cubical geometry this would correspond to the smoke being confined to a volume of 
about 64 cm3 rather than being diluted in the 6000 cm3 piston.  If the same number of particles is generated as for 
the flow case, the initial concentration will be on the order of 50 times higher for the zero-flow case.    This is

The zero flow condition was not in the original design of the SAME hardware but was examined for 11 tests by 
modifying the valve operation in the SAME hardware.  This resulted in a very high concentration of particulate 
where the aging process was accelerated compared to that in the aging chamber at dilute conditions.  An unfortunate 
side effect was that approximately half the smoke was lost from the system because it diffused out of the inlet into 
the MSG volume.  As a result the total particle counts were lower than normal and the TEM grids had few particles.  
It is important to recognize that this condition is unique to low-gravity scenarios.  If one performed the same 
experiment at 1-g, the buoyancy of the rising gases would greatly increase the mixing zone.  So the larger particle 
diameters observed in these zero-flow conditions are important to consider in the development of improved fire 
detection equipment for space vehicles.    
 
For the zero-flow case, the heat is transported primarily by conduction rather than convection.  This is likely to 
result in a significant increase in the gas temperature relative to the case with 8 cm/s air flow.  A striking effect of 
this temperature change is the change in the morphology of the Pyrell smoke from fractal-like clusters with up to 30 
primary spheres for the case with a flow of 8 cm/s to spherical particles for the zero-flow condition (Fig 13). 
 
    
 
SAME Smoke-in-Drums Ground-Based Experiment  
In order to assess whether the size distribution of the smoke is lognormal, detailed particle size distributions 
were measured with a reference instrument.  This cannot be accomplished in low gravity, so this investigation was 
performed with the ground-based engineering SAME hard ware which is identical to the setup on the ISS, 
incorporating the flight aerosol instruments which had been returned to earth.  A Scanning Mobility Particle Sizer 
(SMPS) Spectrometer (3936, TSI, Shoreview, MN, USA) was used as the reference instrument in validation 
experiment.  The SMPS requires a two minute scan through a range of voltages to acquire a high resolution particle 
size distribution; however, the duration of smoke supplied from the SAME aging chamber is at most 30 seconds.  
Therefore, the smoke was collected in an intermediate container which served two purposes.  The first purpose was 
to sufficiently dilute the smoke from the SAME chamber in order to effectively stop coagulation (aging) of the 
smoke particles during the SMPS scans.  The second purpos e was to have a large enough quantity of dilute smoke 
for multiple SMPS scans.  A 55 gallon drum was chosen for this purpose and the SAME smoke-in-drums setup was 
developed to enable SMPS measurements on a portion of the smoke output from the SAME piston chamber.  The 
configuration is shown in Figure 14, which shows the or iginal SAME hardware inside the dashed outline.  One 
DustTrak™ was removed from the original SAME configuration and its portion of the smoke sample was diverted 
from the setup to one of two drums which hold the diluted smoke during multiple 2-minute SMPS measurements.  
One drum collected fresh smoke from the heated sample material and the other drum was filled after a controlled 
aging period in the piston chamber.  Thus both aged and unaged smoke could be measured with the SMPS.

Drum Hardware and Experimental Process 
The two 55 gallon drums were minimally modified for use in the experiment as follows: A muffin fan was bolted 
to the circular drum floor opposite the removable lid.  All other modifications were made to the lid, including feed-
through adapters for tubing and the electrical fan cord, and mounted HEPA filters through which clean air was 
provided for purging.  A four-way crossover valve enable d the drum to be either filled with smoke via a vacuum 
pump preceded by a flow-controlling orifice, or bypassed by the smoke, which effectively isolated the SAME 
hardware from high pressure during the drum purging process.  Transfer of un-aged smoke into the drum began 
when the SAME software commanded the valve opening and lowered the piston in the aging chamber causing half 
of the chamber volume to be expelled (3 liters), with the remainder of the smoke retained in the chamber and 
allowed to age for 12 minutes.  The flow rate into the drum was 1.7 L/min, matching the flow rate of the DustTrak™  
instrument that the drums replaced.  It took less than 2 minut es to transfer the smoke sample into the drum.  Tubing 
from the SAME hardware to the drums was less than one meter in order to minimize transport losses of smoke 
particles.  Initial calculations from previous SAME data indi cated that for all materials, the aerosol concentration in 
the drum would be less than 2 × 10 4 particles/cm3, which is below the rule-of-thumb threshold concentration of 
106 particles/cm3.  Below this level, coagulation can be neglected since it will occur at a very slow rate. 15  Thus it 
could be assumed that very little aging took place in th e drum during the SMPS measurements of un-aged smoke.  
The drum concentration was well within the counting range of the SMPS so no additional dilution was required for

the measurements.  During each SMPS sample, the volume of air removed was between 0.5 % and 1.5 % of the 
drum volume and a correspondingly small number of particles were removed so the drum aerosol concentration was 
relatively constant during the measurements.  Any make-up air needed during the sampling was drawn in through 
the HEPA filters on the drum lid.  The fan in the drum was used to mix the smoke and prevent stratification which 
could skew the SMPS measurements.  First, a 10:1 sheath -to-aerosol flow ratio was used for three consecutive 
measurements with high fidelity giving particle sizes up to 660 nm.  Three subsequent samples were taken with a 
flow rate ratio of 5:1, in order to reach the largest meas urable SMPS particle size of 1000 nm.  Considering that 
aging increases particle size, the high er flow rate ratio (smaller range) give s results for only a portion of the true 
aged size distribution for most materials in this experiment.  Therefore the larger range is important for 
measurements in spite of the low resolution.  After six SMPS scans at two different flow rates, the drum was purged 
with a continuous flow of HEPA-filtered house air at appr oximately 309 kPa-g (45 psig), which was exhausted into 
a fume hood.  An additional P-Trak™ was used to indicate when the drum concentration was below 30 
particles/cm3, which was considered ‘clean’.  One set of SMPS measurements for one smoke sample (both aged and 
unaged) was accomplished in approximately 30 minutes.   
 
SMPS Results for Spherical Smoke Aerosols 
 Five SAME materials were tested in the dr um configuration at two temperature levels, 
baseline and high temperature.  Typical particle size distributions from the ground testing 
validation experiments of the un-aged and aged smoke for the more spherical aerosols are plotted 
in Figs. 6 through 8.  Pyrell® and Teflon® are not spherical aerosols and thus are not relevant to 
the moment method approach.  The mean particle size distributions are shown in the upper plots 
which have open plot marker symbols for unaged smoke and solid symbols for aged smoke.  The 
plotted lines represent a lognormal curve-fit with the MATLAB Statistics Toolbox function 
‘nlinfit’ which performs non-linear least squares regression with the Levenberg-Marquardt 
algorithm (MATLAB version R2012a, The MathWorks, Inc.).  Residual plots, shown also in the 
lower portion of Figs. 15 through 17 are aligned with the corresponding size distribution plots 
above, showing the deviations from the lognormal fits.  This visual test for ‘goodness-of-fit’ 
would result in randomly scattered residual points both above and below zero, for a good 
lognormal fit.  It is common to observe a wedge-shaped spread of residuals, as in Kapton (Fig. 
15), where the tails of the distribution have mostly small residual values, with a wider spread of 
residuals around the peak diameter.  In general, the spread of the residuals is more compact for 
Kapton and lamp wick, indicating a better lognormal fit for these materials.  Note that the 
Kapton residuals are mostly positive up to 70 nm, which indicates that the data are less steep 
than the lognormal fit.  The lamp wick residual plot (Fig. 16) also shows a small but systematic 
deviation from the lognormal fit, which is evident by the change in sign of the unaged data 
residuals between 500 and 600 nm.  Silicone residual plots (Fig. 17) show the least randomness, 
which indicates that the lognormal fit is less valid.  The residuals change signs on both sides of 
the peak, indicating  a shoulder in the small sizes (residuals go from positive to negative), the 
peak is offset from the fit (positive residuals around 400 nm) and the data is steeper than the 
lognormal fit in the large sizes (negative residuals).  Some samples have an initial uptick in the 
small diameter tail, which is believed to be a sampling anomaly in the SMPS, possibly an artifact 
from the previous sample, as the scans were performed in rapid succession.  This anomaly did 
not have a significant effect on the parameters obtained in the fitting of the SMPS data.

Limitations of Aerosol Instrument Measurement Ranges  
Calibration of SAME instruments was intended to empirically account for differences in the 
ranges of the instruments.  In the ground valida tion tests, however, the truncated distribution 
formula (equation 13) can shed light on th e limitations and unce rtainty of the SMPS 
measurement range for the fuels te sted.  Particularly when the particle size distributions are 
converted to surface area or volume distributions, the percentage of the distribution that is 
lacking can be significant.  Furthermore,  the upper end of the SMPS size distribution 
measurement may not be as reliable because it can be affected by poor counting statistics and 
these bins are more susceptible to multiple charge  correction errors.  Therefore it is prudent to 
compare a more conservative upper SMPS limit of 700 nm along with the full recorded range to 
1000 nm, to see the effect of the SMPS measuremen t range.  Thus, if we were to consider the 
SMPS data most reliable (least uncertainty) in  the range from 23 to 700 nm, the truncated 
distribution formula for Mp,rel can indicate what percentage of the distribution would be captured 
with this limitation.  Figure 10 shows the percentage of the distributions captured by the SMPS 
for two example materials.  Kapton is the be st candidate for SMPS va lidation, as the highest 
percentages of each type of distribution are w ithin the SMPS measurement range. For example, 
considering both the conservative  700 nm limit and the 1000 nm limit, the bar graph indicates 
that 98% to 100% of the distribution has been measured.  Silicone smoke is not a good candidate 
for SMPS validation because of th e lack of measurement range, pa rticularly when converting to 
surface and volume size distributions.  Particularly  in the volume distribution in Fig. 23 (right

graph), the black bar representing a 1000 nm upper size limit is only at 40%, indicating that 60% 
of the distribution is missed by the instrument, but when losses are considered and a range of 700 
nm is relied upon, approximately 20% of the distribution is captured (the white bar).

Log-probability Plot 
The log-probability plot is a graphical technique used to assess lognormality of an aerosol.  
Discrete data from the SMPS size bins and TEM size distributions are plotted on the probability 
scale.  Lognormal distributions will be a straight line, and volume and number size distributions 
should be parallel, indicating that σg is the same for both distributions but with different means.  
Extremes on the graphs can be neglected in the log probability plots for number distributions 
when they deviate from the straight line fit for 5% or less of the extremes of the probability scale 
(Hinds, 1999).  For the SMPS data, these deviations are the result of poor counting statistics in 
the large diameter tail and lack of measurement range (for lamp wick and silicone), which 
particularly affects the volume distribution plots.  Thus the volume distribution plot will display 
a line that is slightly curved at the large sizes, which corresponds to a lack of linearity of the 
number distribution line beyond 95% of the distribution.  Figures 24 and 25 show log-probability 
plots for Kapton®, silicone and lamp wick at high temperature.  The plotted cumulative 
frequencies are quite linear for Kapton® and the number and volume distribution lines are nearly 
parallel.  The log probability plot for silicone is not linear and thus fits a lognormal distribution 
poorly.  The lognormal fit and the residual plot in Fig. 17 reflect the same result, where the data 
are steeper than the fit curve for large diameters and less steep than the fit results for smaller 
diameters, thus the log probability plot on the right side in Fig. 24 has deviations from the 
straight line fits at both the smallest and largest percentages of the distributions.

Sample heating temperature derivation 
Sample heating temperature is one of the key parameters that dictate the properties of generated smoke particles. 
When studying effects of gravity on the smoke properties, we want to compare smokes generated at the same 
temperature. For SAME and SAMER, during a test, the so ftware controls the temperature via the resistance of 
heating wire. It is true that for the same wire coil, co nstant wire resistance means constant wire temperature.  
Traditionally, test conditions are specified by Rt/R0, the ratio between the resistance of heated wire over the 
resistance of the wire at room temper ature. Thus, before each run, the samp le wire resistance is measured, then 
multiplied by this parameter to get the target resistance for the control circuitry. Although, Rt/R0 can uniquely 
define the temperature, it is not clear what actual sample  temperature is. Since the wire resistance is one of the 
parameters that are logged in the en gineering data sheet which makes it possible to derive actual temperature from 
the logged resistances. However, when deriving wire temperatures, one has to take the fact into account that the wire 
length varies from sample to sample and so called room temperature varies too. After the heating temperatures were 
obtained, it is surprising that for the same R t/R0, the actual heating temperature di fference can be as large as 30 
degrees Celsius. The following is how this is carried out.  
 
 
SAME heater temperature modeling.

Objective: 
 
It was identified that each sample has a significant length of leading section of the resistive wire. This section does not touch the 
sample material and is exposed in air flow. Thus the temperature of this leading section is different from the portion of the wire 
that contacts the sample material. The control circuitry only controls the total resistance of the heating wire, not individual 
portion of the wire. 
 
Our goal is to find the temperature of the wire that is in contact with the sample material. 
 
Formulation: 
Hypothesis:  the temperature difference between the two portions of the wire is caused by different convection heat transfer from 
the two. The wire that is in contact with the sample has less heat loss from the convection heat transfer because about half of its 
surface area is covered by the sample material. 
 
Assumptions and simplifications: 
1) Assume the entire wire consists of two distinct portions, one is in air (portion 1) and the other (portion 2) is in touch 
with the sample so that only half of the wire area is exposed to air.    
2) Uniform cross section area of the wire, so the resistance is proportional to the length and the resistivity of the wire. 
3) Resistivity is a known function of temperature. 
4) Temperature distribution inside wire is uniform. 
5) Newton convective heat transfer equation applies to both sections but with different coefficients.  Although the port 2 is 
half exposed in air where convective equation works and half in contact with sample where transient conduction heat 
transfer should be used, for the sake of simplicity, we lump the two mechanisms together and use convection only with 
a modified heat transfer coefficient.

I. Introduction 
ppropriate design of fire detection systems requires knowledge of both the expected signature of the events to 
be detected and the background levels of the measured parameters.  Terrestrial fire detection systems have been 
developed based on extensive study of terrestrial fires. 1, 2  Unfortunately there is no corresponding data set for 
spacecraft fires and consequently the fire detectors in current spacecraft were developed based upon terrestrial 
designs.  There are a number of factors that can be expected to affect the particle size distribution of the smoke from 
spacecraft fires. The absence of buoyant flow in low-gravit y increases the residence time in microgravity fires and 
increases the transit time from the reaction zone to the detector. 3 Microgravity fires have been found to have 
radically different structure from their normal-gravity (a.k.a. 1-g) counterparts.  The limited options available to 
respond to a spacecraft fire increase the importance of early detection.  Finally the materials used in spacecraft are 
different from typical terrestrial applications where smoke properties were previously evaluated.  All of these effects 
can be expected to change the smoke particle size distribution.  The objective of this work was to make sufficient 
measurements of smoke from spacecraft fires to enable improved design of future detectors.  
Smoke Background 
Smoke is a general term that encompasses aerosol materials produced by a number of processes.  In particular it 
can include unburned, recondensed, original polymer or pyrolysis products that can be either liquid or solid, 
hydrocarbon soot, condensed water vapor, and ash particles.  Soot particles dominate the smoke particulate in 
established flaming fires while unburned pyrolysis produc ts and recondensed polymer fragments are produced by 
smoldering and pyrolysis in the early stage of fire growth.  Given the constrained space on any spacecraft, the target 
for the fire detection system  is necessarily the early phase and not es tablished flaming fires; consequently, the 
primary target for detection is the pyrolysis products and not the soot.   
Prior spacecraft systems are summarized in more  detail in papers by Friedman and Urban. 4, 5  In the Mercury, 
Gemini and Apollo missions, the crew quarters were limited and mission durations were short, consequently it was 
considered reasonable that the astronauts would rapidly detect any fire. The Skylab module, however, included 
approximately 30 UV-sensing fire detectors. 4 These devices were limited to line-of-sight and were reported to have 
difficulties with false alarms.  The Space Shuttle Detectors were based upon ioni zation fire detector technology, the 
most advanced technology available at the time and used an inertial separator designed to eliminate particles larger 
than 1-2 micrometers. The International Space Station (ISS) smoke de tectors use near-IR forward scattering, 
rendering them most sensitive to particles larger than a mi crometer, outside of the range of sensitivity of the shuttle 
detector. As described by Friedman4 there have been six overheat and failed component events in the NASA Orbiter 
fleet in addition to several similar incidents that have occurr ed on the ISS. None of these events spread into a real 
fire but as mission durations increase, the likelihood of failures increases. The experience on Mir in 1997 has shown 
that failure of oxygen generation systems can have significant consequences. As a result, improved understanding of 
spacecraft fire detection is critically needed.6  
Previous work on smoke particles from low-gravity sources by Urban et al. 5 found that the particulate produced 
by low-gravity flames (soot or unburned fuel particles) tends to have larger size particles than in normal gravity.  
Results from the CSD (Comparative Soot Diagnostics) Experiment 5 which studied smoke properties in low-gravity 
from several spacecraft materials suggested  that liquid smoke particles could achieve sizes larger than 1 µm while 
solid particulate remained in the sub-micrometer range.  However, the CSD experiment did not produce sufficient 
data concerning the size of the liquid smoke particles to guide detector design. The combined impact of these limited 
results and theoretical predictions is that, as opposed to  extrapolation from 1-g data, direct knowledge of low-g 
combustion particulate is needed for more confident design of smoke detectors for spacecraft.   
II. SAME Experiment 
To address the limited data from the CSD experiment concerning the likely size of spacecraft smoke particulate, 
another experiment was developed: the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME).  The SAME experiment 
sought to avoid the problems experienced by the CSD experiment by obtaining the particulate size statistics on-orbit 
with a reduced dependence upon sample return to Earth.  This is a challenging endeavor because existing aerosol 
instrumentation is typically large, incompatible with spacecraft experiment constraints, and some systems require 
substantial sample return to Earth.  As will be described below, an alternative approach was employed that used 
three discrete instruments to measure separate moments of the size distribution.  When combined, these moments 
provide useful aggregate statistics of the size distribution.  The measurements were made using smoke generated by 
overheated spacecraft materials in much the same manner as the CSD experiment however the sample temperature, 
flow field, and particle aging time were more rigorously controlled in the SAME experiment.  The experiment flew

Calibration of the moment instruments was essential to properly interpret the flight data and was performed on

For SAME-2, one of the DustTrak devices was replace d by a new device the MPASS (Multi-Parameter Aerosol 
Scattering Sensor) which is an optical scattering sensor , employing two detectors pl aced at fixed angles.  The 
underlying design and performance have been reported previously. 12 The basic configuration is similar to the 
DustTrak, however, the MPASS has two angles of detection and it can measure two moment approximate moment 
quantities specifically the 3 rd and 2 nd moments.  Further, the optical geomet ry is optimized using a Mie-scattering 
model for aerosols with light scattering properties typical of smoke: i) geometric mean diameters from 0.1 – 1.0 
microns; ii) geometric standard deviations of 1.6 – 1.9; iii) the aerosols have lognormal size distributions and vi) a 
fixed, real value for refractive index of 1.6.  This device was included as a technology demonstration of an aerosol 
sensor that measures two moments simultaneously.  The underlying assumption is that by measuring two moments 
of the aerosol it is possible to correct  the smoke detector signal for the pa rticle size, unlike previous spacecraft 
smoke detectors which are limited to a single moment measurement10.  This will enable the alarm to be less sensitive 
to larger particles that are typical of dust. The relative advantage of this approach was discussed in more detail in a 
prior paper13.

G. Experimental Results 
Over 100 sample materials were tested.  These were comprised of samples of 6 materials: Teflon™, Kapton™, 
Pyrell™, silicone rubber, cellulose (lamp wick), and dibutyl-phthalate deposited on a porous wick. The test 
conditions included multiple sample temperatures and air flow rates.  The baseline air flow rate was 8 cm/s with 
runs conducted at rates down to 2 cm/s with a limited set conducted with no airflow while the sample was heated.  
The sample temperatures were based on the pyrolysis properties of the material and were thus material specific.  The 
baseline temperature was selected to produce 1 to 2 mg of weight loss in 60 seconds and have reasonable signal on 
each of the moment instruments.  To examine the effect of sample temper ature, additional higher temperature 
conditions were also selected that would not saturate th e moment instruments. The TEM girds recovered from the 
thermal precipitators on SAME-1 were unfortunately cont aminated with extraneous particles whose origin is 
currently under investigation. For SAME-2 more rigorous assembly controls were followed and numerous good 
particle images were obtained.  For typical runs, the partic le concentrations were a few million particles / cc and the 
mass concentrations were 2 to 15 mg/m 3 however there were runs with fewer particles.  For these conditions, the 
typical numbers of particles sampled by the instruments were in the billions although for the test with the lowest 
particle concentrations the sample sizes were of the order of several million particles. 
1. Moment Instrument Results 
Geometric mean, count mean, and average mass diameter re sults from the moment instruments for baseline runs 
are presented in Table 1.  As desc ribed above, the count mean diameter  and the diameter of average mass 
measurements are independent of the nature of the size distribution however, the calculation of the geometric mean 
diameter and the geometric standard deviation ( σg) depend on the assumption of a log-normal distribution.  This 
assumption cannot be directly tested with the available da ta since this would require a device that can separate the 
particles into size bins,  However, there are two indications that the distribution can be approximated by a log-
normal distribution.  In the cases listed below, the count mean diameter is less than the diameter of average mass 
which is a necessary condition for a log-normal distribution (See Fig. 1).  The second indication is that the geometric 
standard deviations are all physically reasonable (i.e. greater than 1 (see Eq. 3) and less than approximately 3.5 
which is the practical limit on the magnitude of aerosol ge ometric standard deviation).  The aging results show a 
substantial increase in the observed diam eters.  As expected the increase in th e count mean diameter is greater than 
the corresponding increase in th e diameter of average mass.  This can be understood since coagulation consists of 
particle collisions joining two particles.  For a polydisper se aerosol, these collisions usually involve the collision of 
one of the smallest (high mobility) particles with the larg est (high cross-section) par ticles. This collision has little 
effect on the size of the large particle but it removes the smaller particles from the size distribution.  This has a 
larger effect on the count mean diameter since it is linear in diameter while the diameter of average mass varies with 
the cube root of the diameter. Theoretical predictions suggest that this process will produce a near lognormal 
distribution and that the standard deviation will tend toward a self-preserving distribution with a value of 1.32.14

2. MPASS Results 
The MPASS was included in SAME-2 to demonstrate the effectiveness of a two-moment smoke detector. 
Because of how they are used, a smoke  detector is not calibrated for speci fic materials and instead has a single 
calibration for all conditions. The objective is to maintain a flat sensor response, regardless of the type of smoke or 
the particle size so the signal is proportional only to a se lected moment (e.g. mass or number concentration).  The 
approach used was to derive correlations to predict the smoke number concentration and mass concentration from 
the MPASS output.  This correlation was made using the other SAME measurements (number and mass 
concentration) as a reference.  A least-squares, third-order, correlation was computed on all test points with a signal 
to noise ratio greater than 2 independent of all other parameters (e.g. material, heating rate, and aging time). 
 
The results are shown in figures 9 and 10, for prediction of the mass concentration and the number 
concentration, respectively.  Ideally th ese response graphs should be horizont al lines.  The norm alized output is 
plotted along with the normalized correlation result as  a function of geometric m ean diameter. Ideally the 
normalized result should be horizontal lines. The uniformity of response (scatter) is expressed by the least squares 
variance relative to the mean ( Δ) and is shown in the legend.  Both figures show that the correlation decreases the 
relative variance by roughly a factor of at least 2 relative to that provided by a conventional single-output sensor.  
The resulting variance for the mass response is substantially  lower than for the number concentration.  This is 
consistent with the fact that the original optimizati on of the MPASS was to mass concentration not to number 
concentration.  Thus with appropriate processing, the MPASS output can be proportional to either the number 
concentration or the mass concentration over a wide range of particle sizes and material compositions.  This 
independence demonstrates that by combining 2 moments the MPASS is able to scale its response to the particle 
size being sampled giving a more accurate indication of the amount of smoke present than a single moment detector. 
The MPASS therefore has the ability to discern the difference between a strong signal from a high smoke 
concentration and a strong signal from a lower concentration of very large dust particles, a feature which can 
minimize false smoke detector alarms.

3. TEM Results 
Overall, 72 particle samples were taken on Transmission Electron Microscope (TEM) grids using the thermal 
precipitator.  These samples were imaged with a TEM to evaluate the particle morphology as a function of flow 
conditions, material and heating level.  Overall, silicone rubber and DBP presented no particles that were visible via 
TEM, presumably because the particles were condensed liquid that evaporated before they could be imaged in the 
TEM.  Figure 11 presents typical images for the major materials. 
 
 
As seen in Table 1, aging did increase the average partic le size, however this level of change is not readily 
visible in the TEM images, instead the mo st visible change is the disappearance of  the smallest particles.  (Fig 12)  
As described in the discussion of Table 1, this is consistent with expectations since the smaller particles have the 
highest mobility and consequently are readily incorporated in to the larger particles. Particularly for the semi-liquid 
particles, this absorption of the smallest particles into larger  particles is expected to have little or no apparent effect 
on the size of the larger particles b ecause the diameter is the cube root of  the volume. In th e case of non-liquid 
particles, the smallest particles will ne vertheless be unlikely to be visible via TEM when they are attached to larger 
particles.

4. Impact of flow on particle morphology 
As the samples are heated by the wire, chemical bonds are broken and gaseous products are 
released via pyrolysis.  These products may include partially oxidized species resulting from the 
reaction with oxygen. As the gases move from the wire, the temperature and species 
concentration will decrease as a result of conduction/diffusion and convection.  With the 
decrease in temperature, the super saturation ratio of the pyrolysis gas will pass a critical stage 
and nucleation of smoke particles will occur.  These smoke nuclei grow rapidly from the 
condensation of the pyrolysis gases.  The time scale for the nucleation and condensation is on the 
order of ms or less.  Over a longer time scale, the growing smoke particles undergoing Brownian 
motion collide and stick together in a process known as coagulation.  This process may continue 
for time scales of up to 103 s.  If the particles are liquid, the colliding particles will coalesce and 
form larger droplets.  This is the case for the lampwick, silicone rubber, and Kapton smokes (Fig. 
11).  If the particles are solid, they will retain their structure as they stick resulting in an 
agglomerate structure composed of many primary particles connected in a low density fractal-
like structure.  This is the case for the Teflon and Pyrell smokes (Fig. 11). 
 
Key parameters affecting the smoke properties of the smoke produced here are the low-gravity 
condition, the convective flow past the heated wire, the wire temperature, and the aging time.  As 
the wire temperature increases, more of the sample will be pyrolyzed and these gases will 
subsequently condense on the nuclei leading to a larger mass concentration of the aerosol and a 
larger diameter of average mass.   
 
An increase in the convective flow for a fixed wire temperature is expected to result in an 
increase in the pyrolysis rate and thus an increase in the mass concentration of the aerosol.  Some 
results follow this trend with silicone rubber, lampwick, and Pyrell increasing slightly with flow 
while Teflon and Kapton decrease.  A possible explanation is that holding the wire temperature 
fixed does not necessarily mean that the sample surface temperature distribution is precisely the 
same at different air flow speeds.  Although these are expected to be small variations, given the 
exponential dependence of the pyrolysis kinetics on temperature, changes in the heat transport 
environment could change the sample surface temperature between the wire coils.

A case of special interest is the case of zero-flow.  The transport for the zero-flow case in μ-g is 
controlled by molecular diffusion and thermal expansion.  Over a period of 60 seconds, the gases 
would diffuse a distance on the order of 4 cm.  Assuming a cubical geometry this would 
correspond to the smoke being confined to a volume of about 64 cm3 rather than being diluted in 
the 6000 cm3 piston.  If the same number of particles is generated as for the flow case, the initial 
concentration will be on the order of 50 times higher for the zero-flow case.    This is expected to 
lead to more coagulation and a larger particle size.  It is found for all of the materials the 
diameter of average mass is 30 % to 40 % larger for the zero-flow tests compared to the flow 
tests.   
 
The zero flow condition was not in the original design of the SAME hardware but was examined 
for 11 tests by modifying the valve operation in the SAME hardware.  This resulted in a very 
high concentration of particulate where the aging process was accelerated compared to that in the 
aging chamber at dilute conditions.  An unfortunate side effect was that approximately half the 
smoke was lost from the system because it diffused out of the inlet into the MSG volume.  As a 
result the total particle counts were lower than normal and the TEM grids had few particles.  It is 
important to recognize that this condition is unique to low-gravity scenarios.  If one performed 
the same experiment at 1-g, the buoyancy of the rising gases would greatly increase the mixing 
zone.  So the larger particle diameters observed in these zero-flow conditions are important to 
consider in the development of improved fire detection equipment for space vehicles.    
 
For the zero-flow case, the heat is transported primarily by conduction rather than convection.  
This is likely to result in a significant increase in the gas temperature relative to the case with 8 
cm/s air flow.  A striking effect of this temperature change is the change in the morphology of 
the Pyrell smoke from fractal-like clusters with up to 30 primary spheres for the case with a flow 
of 8 cm/s to spherical particles for the zero-flow condition (Fig 13).

smoke particles are evident for the five spacecraft material s that were tested.  For the conditions of the SAME 
experiment, all samples produced significant numbers of sub-micron particulate that are readily detected using an 
ionization smoke detector. However, the aging results sugg est that some materials such as silicone rubber can 
produce smoke that can reach sizes better detected by light scattering techniques. The zero flow conditions produced 
smoke particles that were 2 to 3 times larger than those produced at the nominal 8 cm/s  flow rate. Since spacecraft 
fire conditions include an even wider array of materials than those tested here and a broader range of flow and 
temperature conditions, broad smoke aerosol size distributions can be expected from credible pre-fire overheat 
events. These results suggest that detection methods that can measure more than one moment of the size distribution 
may show more successful detection and false alarm rejec tion than single moment detectors. The results from the 
prototype 2-moment detector (MPASS) were very encouraging in this respect with the technique showing real 
potential as a means to respond to a broad particle range while avoiding excessive false alarms from nuisance 
sources.  The TEM result demonstrated that fire particulate can be expected to have  a broad range of morphologies 
influenced by heating rate, material and flow conditions.

2.2 SAME Experiment Background 
Since the very beginning of the manned space flight program, NASA engineers and scientists have gone to great lengths to 
prevent fires from occurring on spacecraft. They have done this by adapting fire safety systems and procedures developed 
on Earth to the unique conditions and operating environment of spacecraft. However, microgravity combustion experiments 
have shown that fire can behave very differently in space and the best methods to prevent, detect, and extinguish fires on a 
spacecraft may be very different than those used on Earth. 
In 2000, NASA's Bioastronautics Initiative began with the objective of ensuring and enhancing the health, safety, and 
performance of humans in space. As part of this effort, the  Life Support and Habitation Branch at NASA Glenn Research 
Center is responsible for developing and implementing a research plan to significantly improve fire safety on spacecraft and 
in space habitats. This goal will be achieved by applying a significant amount of fundamental knowledge and the 
experimental capability of microgravity research to spacecraft fire safety questions. 
Spacecraft smoke detectors must detect smoke with a variety of particulate types. Hydrocarbon fuels typically produce soot, 
while overheated plastics produce droplets of recondensed polymer fragments. Paper and silicone rubber produce a smoke 
that is composed of liquid droplets of recondensed pyrolysis products. Differences in the nucleation and growth processes 
for these different types of smokes create particles that have different sizes and properties. 
The Comparative Soot Diagnostics (CSD) experiment that flew in the Glovebox on STS-75 demonstrated that the  smokes 
with solid particulates created in microgravity formed longer chains, and aggregated into larger particles than those created 
in normal Earth gravity. This is surmised to have occurred because of the increased residence time in the high concentration 
smoke regions and to have affected the responses of the two spacecraft smoke detectors (ISS and STS) utilized in that 
experiment. 
To develop smoke detectors that are sensitive to the type and size of smoke particles that will be encountered in 
microgravity and to allow them to distinguish between dust and smoke, better knowledge of the size distribution and 
morphology of the particulates is required. 
2.3 SAME Experiment Objectives 
The major goal of this experiment is to quantify the sizes that the liquid smoke particulates achieve in microgravity and to 
relate the droplet size and distribution to the smoke generation and smoke transport conditions in the experiment. This will 
be accomplished by extending the Comparative Soot Diagnostics (CSD) concept to provide a particulate count and mass 
density determination to the diagnostic array used to analyze these liquid smokes. The experimental design and practical 
application of this data will be enhanced by the development of a numerical code that will predict the smoke droplet growth 
as a function of the fuel pyrolysis rate, the thermodynamic properties of the pyrolysis vapor, and the flow environment. 
The SAME experiment has the following (listed) objectives: 
1. Make measurements of three moments of the particle size distribution for the μg smoke from several 
materials found in spacecraft considering the effects of sample temperature, air flow, smoke residence time 
(near the source) and smoke aging. The primary targets are materials that produce liquid smoke particulate 
but solid smoke producers will also be considered.  
2. Make measurements of the effect of µg and 1-g on the size distribution of liquid aerosol smokes (using an 
idealized smoke e.g. DBT) to provide data for numerical model comparison.   
3. Evaluate the performance in µg of the two existing U.S. spacecraft smoke detector designs for the test 
conditions. 
4. Evaluate other smoke detection/sensing devices at NASA’s request for the test materials 
2.4 SAME “Firsts” for NASA 
• Measurements of microgravity smoke: Diagnostics such as the P-Trak and the DustTrak will be used to measure 
particle count and particle mass concentration, respectively.  Both devices are manufactured by TSI.  With the aid of 
these instruments (and others), microgravity smoke will be characterized. 
• The use of rapid prototype materials for manned flight experiment hardware. 
• Use of an automatic, remotely adjustable, ‘particulate friendly’ dilution system.

2.5 The SAME Risk mitigation experiment – DAFT  
The objective for the risk mitigation experiment, DAFT (Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test), is to provide a 
microgravity technology demonstration of the P-Trak Ultrafine Particle Counter manufactured by TSI.  The P-Trak is a 
hand held air quality monitor which is capable of counting particles whose mean diameter is in the range of 1.0 to 0.05 
microns. 
After extensive market research performed by both the Engineering and Science teams, it has been determined that the P-
Trak is the only commercially available hardware that can perform this particle count while maintaining the weight, 
resource, and space limitations for an MSG experiment.   
P-Trak measures particle number concentrations in real-time  while storing that data in a memory maintained by an on-
board battery. These measurements are made in units of particles per cubic centimeter (pt/cm3) versus traditional aerosol 
measurements of milligrams per cubic meter (mg/m3) made by photometers.  P-Trak operates by using the particles in the 
aerosol as seeds to condense droplets of alcohol (a condensate nuclei counter).  These droplets have many times the average 
diameter of the original particles, and may, therefore, be easily counted with standard optical techniques.  The potential 
problem is that these droplets are directed through a nozzle to facilitate the counting, and some of these droplets (a 
predictable percentage) collide with the walls and form a film. In a gravity environment, this film is recycled by ‘falling’ 
down hill. 
In microgravity, the distinct possibility exists that these droplets will form a film that will bridge and block the nozzle, 
effectively plugging the flow of droplets and preventing the device from functioning, or obscuring the optics.  Furthermore, 
there is some concern that the droplets inside the optics chamber may get trapped in an internal circular motion and be 
counted more than once, producing an erroneously high count. 
The modification that was implemented in order to counteract these potential problems was: 60. 0.006” grooves were 
machined down the length of the inside of the condenser.  These grooves were designed to provide a mechanism in which 
the smoke particle/ alcohol mixture can wick its way back to reservoir end to simulate the effects of gravity, hence, 
inhibiting the possibility of the fluid to inhibit the functioning of the unit. 
The modifications to account for and eliminate this problem have been devised and implemented, however, it is not possible 
to test the effectiveness of these modifications in any of the available ground based facilities and/or the KC-135 due to the 
duration of the nominal operation time required (minutes per instance).  This testing, and the verification of the accuracy of 
the instrument functions on orbit, are the core of the DAFT experiment. 
Two P-Trak units are included in DAFT flight hardware, one being only flight hardened, and the other with the modified 
condenser and flight hardened. 
To successfully accomplish P-Trak functional demonstration, additional hardware (which will not be explained in detail 
here) has to be delivered to the ISS. This hardware includes a dust concentration monitor (DustTrak), data cables, fill 
assembly, sample bag assemblies, sample holders, virtual impactor, alcohol reservoir, battery packs, a HEPA filter 
assembly, and appropriate tubing. 
The P-Trak utilizes isopropyl alcohol as a condensate, and its use must therefore, be carefully monitored and requires a 
specific agreement for that use on the ISS which is contained within a Volatile Usage Agreement (VUA) created for the 
experiment.

4.0 SAME CREW INTERFACES 
4.1 Hardware Subsystem Description 
The major planned components of SAME are as follows. They are organized by the assembly level, and the order in which 
they are currently planned to be installed into the MSG.: 
1. Fluids Control Box Assembly (67198MABA220) 
The Fluids Control Box (FCB) installs on the back wall of the MSG in the upper left section. It is a fan cooled 
enclosure made from aluminum that contains most of the fluids control devices and monitoring devices including 
solenoids, pressure regulator, pressure transducers and mass flow controller. It interfaces directly with the MSG 
fluids resources (VES and GN2) and the Power Distribution and Control Unit (PDCU), and distributes the fluids 
resources accordingly. Please refer to the SAME Fluids Schematic (67198PABA000) for more information on its, 
and the other fluids system functions. 
2. Sample Plate Assembly (Experiment Support Plate Assembly) 67198ABA100 
This assembly, when fully integrated, contains all of the major functional systems of SAME. It is a mounting plate 
which includes the mounting hardware for the Sample Carousel, the Thermal Precipitator Unit (TPU), the 
Dynamic Diagnostics Assembly (DDA) and the Aging Chamber Assembly (ACA). Permanently mounted to it 
are: 
• The Smoke Generation Tube 
• The Video Camera and Controller 
• The Sample Positioning system including: 
o the Sample Turning Module 
o the sample engagement  mechanism 
o the sample position indicator 
o the sample positioning lock mechanism 
o the Sample Carousel mounting system

3. Dynamic Diagnostics Assembly (DDA) (67198MDBA165) 
The DDA is attached to the Sample Plate Assembly and the Aging Chamber Assembly by the crew and contains: 
the ISS and STS smoke detectors and the sampling ports that supply the P-Trak Enclosure and the Commercial 
Diagnostics Enclosure (and port(s) added for any additional diagnostics required). The DDA has a very low 
internal volume, and the flow of the sample aerosol through it is controlled by regulating and balancing the 
requirements of the active diagnostics in the DDA with the exhaust rate of the Aging Chamber piston, as 
controlled by its mass flow controller. It also contains a port, protected by a HEPA filter, that is connected to the 
VES for exhaust and purging. 
4. Aging Chamber Assembly (67198MABA150) 
The Aging Chamber Assembly contains the cylindrical, metallic Aging Chamber, the pneumatically activated 
Inlet and Outlet Gate Valves and the Inlet and Outlet Elbows, which connect to the Smoke Generation Tube and 
the DDA, respectively. A Rulon piston, internal to the chamber, moves the sample into and out from the internal 
volume, and that flow is controlled by a mass flow controller which regulates the pressure or vacuum flow 
accordingly.  Sampling ports are provided in the elbows for use by the Thermal Precipitator, and the unit contains 
a Mixing Fan to insure that the contents are homogenous before disbursal to the DDA. 
5. Data Acquisition and Control Unit (DACU) (67198EABA660) 
The DACU is the central control unit for SAME. The baseline software is resident there, and, although many of 
the other packages contain their own relay and control cards, ultimately it is the DACU that interfaces with the 
Ethernet and the MLC to orchestrate the performance of the experiment. It also collects and stores data for 
subsequent downlink through the MSG systems, and controls the MSG Video Recorder to provide a taped record 
of the pyrolysis event. 
6. P-Trak Enclosure (67198MABA500) 
The P-Trak Enclosure is a flight hardened assembly containing a TSI P-Trak modified to take advantage of the 
VES system and to function in a microgravity environment. Although it interfaces with the DDA, the DACU, the 
Fluids Control Unit and the Power Distribution and Control Unit, it is basically a smart box that can operate 
independently and store its own data.  
7. Commercial Diagnostics Enclosure (CDE) (67198MABA600) 
The CDE houses two of the SAME diagnostics, the TSI DustTrak and a First Alert ionization smoke detector. 
Both units have been hardened for flight and have been modified to utilize the VES to drive the sample. The 
DustTrak has also been modified to utilize MSG air to provide its ‘sheath air’ in order to decrease the amount of 
aerosol required by the unit. Like P-Trak, the DustTrak portion of this device can operate independently and store 
its own data. The modified First Alert cannot.  
8. Dynamic Diluter (DD) (67198MABA180) 
The DD is a custom designed component that provides dilution of the aerosol from the DDA before its 
introduction into the P-Trak (and possibly the DustTrak). It works by utilizing a laminar flow element to measure 
the amount of sample being introduced and using that information (from a differential pressure transducer) to 
increase or decrease the diluent flow to achieve the desired concentration. The dilution setpoint may be altered by 
software and adjusts to the desired setting in approximately 5 seconds. 
9. Power Distribution and Control Unit (PDCU) (67198EABA680) 
The PDCU is the central disbursement point for the commands, power distribution and data collection for SAME. 
It contains the power converters, main relays and terminal data connections for the entire system and interfaces the 
DACU with the various systems and devices constituting the experiment.

10. Sample Carousel Assembly (67198MABB400) 
The Sample Carousel Assemblies (5) each contain six (6) Sample Tubes that interface the samples to the Smoke 
Generation Tube and allow the capture of the smoke in the Aging Chamber. Sample Carousels are sequentially 
installed onto the mounting locations on the Sample Plate Assembly, and the mechanisms contained by it identify 
the individual sample numbers, rotate the carousel to the correct position and engage the Sample Tube, which 
allows the sample to be in a position to be energized.  The samples themselves are composed of five (5) materials: 
Teflon, Kapton, Silicone, Cellulose and DiButyl Phthalate (which being a liquid, is contained within a small 
section of cotton lampwick) in small, cylindrical sections, that are wrapped with coils of wire (baseline: stainless 
steel) that both provides the heat energy to the sample when energized and measures its temperature (by its 
varying resistance). 
These samples are removed from the tubes for weighing, both before and after the experiment (before launch and 
after being downmassed) to quantify the actual mass loss during pyrolysis. 
11. Thermal Precipitator Unit (TPU) (67198MABB300) 
The TPU is a device that captures actual samples of the aerosol particulate on Transmission Electron Microscope 
(TEM) grids for examination when returned from the ISS. The units (4) are number matched to the samples in the 
carousel, to take samples from both the Inlet and Outlet Elbows leading to and from the Aging Chamber. 
12. Alcohol Wick Storage Container (67198MABD700) 
The Alcohol Wick Storage Container is a custom manufactured aluminum vessel to contain the alcohol wick 
required by the P-Trak during the time (launch, non-ops) when it is not in direct use. Only one is nominally 
required, but two are included to provide one as a backup. 
13. Hoses 
SAME utilizes ISS GN2 and the VES system both as resources for the experiment process and as systems to 
power its devices. These resources are distributed to the components from the FCU via the hoses, which are 
nominally operated at +/- 15 psig. In order to conserve weight and volume, and provide ease of operation, acrylic 
hoses and quick disconnects will be used for the distribution of pressure and vacuum throughout the system (not 
typical Teflon with stainless steel overbraid). 
14. Harnessing 
All harnessing will conform to applicable standards and be designed to minimize the crew time needed to make 
the required experiment connections, without sacrificing reliability. 
15. SAME Service Kit 
This is a place holder. SAME has not yet defined any servicing requirements. 
4.2 Video Recording Devices 
Video recordings of the smoke evolution process are very important for establishing proper operation of the test apparatus 
and for debugging the system operation.  Furthermore, the video provides a helpful demonstration of the variability in 
smoke evolution. Experience with CSD showed dramatic cases where clearly visible smoke streams were not always 
detectable by the smoke detectors while invisible smoke streams were readily detected. Normal video resolution is 
acceptable if the smoke is illuminated by forward scattered light from an appropriate light source. Video will be viewed on 
and recorded by the MSG video Monitor/Recorder. 
4.3 On-Orbit Crew Operational Functions 
The crew will be asked to assemble the experiment from provided subsections, load software, reload Sample Carousels, 
Thermal Precipitator Modules, and alcohol for the particle counter, enter parameters, initiate the experiment, and 
disassemble the experiment.

5.0 SAME SOFTWARE CONTROL 
5.1 Software Controlled Operational Functions 
The DACU is the central point for SAME control.  It is ultimately responsible for all experiment operations and interfacing 
with the environment external to SAME.  It contains all of the logic necessary to autonomously operate the experiment as 
well as receive, validate, and process commands from the MSG.  The DACU periodically transmits the status of the Smoke 
system to the MSG, which then forwards it to the ground.   The software can autonomously control the progress of 
preprogrammed test, manage and store all science and system files on the local data storage medium, control the MSG 
video recorder capturing Smoke images, and copy the files to the MLC for downlink.  The software inside the DACU is 
also responsible for providing diagnostic information and manual control of all sensors and controls using the GSE port. 
Please refer to the SAME Baseline Software Requirements Document (SAME-DOC-004) for more detail. 
5.2 Data Collection 
Data is collected and stored in the DACU until it is time to downlink the information.  The Thermal Precipitator Module, 
which collects samples of the smoke, will be bagged and returned for analysis.  Sample Carousels are retained so that the 
samples can be weighed after return to Earth. 
6.0 SAME OPERATIONS 
6.1 Operations Flow 
1. Experiment Setup- The experiment will be shipped in individual subassemblies that will be assembled inside of 
the MSG.  Parts will be inserted through the MSG side ports starting with the upper, back components.  After 
the MSG ports are covered and the rack is returned to nominal position, the Experiment Software is installed 
onto the MSG Laptop. 
2. Perform Experiment- The first steps in performing the experiment are to load the desired Sample Carousel, load 
or replenish the alcohol wick in the particle counter, and install a new Thermal Precipitator Module.  Next, the 
start-up check out routine is performed.  After the uplink parameters are sent, the experiment is initiated.  Then, 
the baseline uplink parameters are modified, as required, for the next test and the experiment is initiated again 
until all six samples in the Sample Carousel have been used.  The next number matched Sample Carousel and 
Thermal Precipitator Module will then be loaded and the experiment will continue as such until complete. 
3. Shutdown and Repack Experiment- When all the Sample Carousels have been used and all the experiments 
have been performed,  the final Sample Carousel and Thermal Precipitator Module will be capped and bagged.  
In reverse order of installation, the experiment hardware will be repackaged for downmassing. 
6.2 Detailed Operations 
Please refer to the SAME Operations Concept Document (SAME-DOC-009) for a more detailed description of all 
Operations functions. 
6.3 Timeline 
Since the experiment is designed for operations controlled from the ground, once the components have been installed in the 
MSG, timeline concerns have mainly to do with the acquisition of command windows and with weekly or semi weekly 
service sessions by the crew.  
SAME will follow the standard ISS procedures for scheduling activities aboard the station including OCR and iURC 
submittals and conferences with the ISS Cadre.

7.1 Overall Strategy 
Safety analysis is being performed for the SAME (formerly Smoke) hardware in accordance with the safety policies and 
safety requirements for flight hardware (NSTS1700.7B and ISS Addendum). This assessment is being prepared using 
NSTS 13830C as a guideline for data submittal. Hazards not eliminated by design are addressed in either the latest revision

Hazard Report, JSC 542B. For the most part, the SAME experiment uses generic hazard controls for electrical power
